title: The Character I Almost Overlooked: Peninnah
paragraphs: The Character I Almost Overlooked: Peninnah
She had what Hannah begged God for.
And still, Peninnah is not remembered as blessed.
She is remembered as a wound.

In 1 Samuel 1, Peninnah had children. Hannah did not. In a culture where motherhood carried deep honor, Peninnah had the visible proof of fruitfulness. Hannah had tears. Peninnah had sons and daughters. Hannah had a closed womb. And instead of covering Hannah’s grief with compassion, Peninnah turned her blessing into a blade. Scripture says she “provoked her severely, to make her miserable”. Not once. Year after year. (1 Samuel 1:6–7)
That is chilling.
Because you can be fruitful in one area and still be cruel in spirit.
You can carry evidence of blessing and still not carry the heart of God.

Peninnah is the kind of character many people skip past because Hannah’s pain is louder. But Peninnah matters, because she exposes something ugly in the human heart: the temptation to use our strength to torment someone at their weakest point. To flaunt what others lack. To turn another person’s silent sorrow into our private stage for superiority.
But here’s what we miss.
Peninnah is not just a villain in Hannah’s story. She is a mirror for us.

Not because most of us will openly mock a barren woman. But because many people know how to provoke. Subtle jabs. Weaponized blessings. Spiritual pride. Hidden competition. The smugness that says, “Look what I have that you don’t.” Sometimes the cruelest people are not empty people. They are full people with unhealed hearts.
That is why blessing without grace becomes dangerous.

Peninnah had children.
Hannah had prayer.

Peninnah had proof.
Hannah had dependence.
And in the end, it was Hannah’s brokenness that became the birthplace of Samuel.
That is the scandal of grace: God often does His deepest work through the one being humiliated, not the one appearing strong.

And before we point too hard at Peninnah, we need to let the Gospel search us. Have we ever mocked someone’s weakness? Envied someone’s pain because it made us feel stronger? Used our marriage, our ministry, our platform, our children, our money, our beauty, our open doors, to silently exalt ourselves over someone still waiting on God?
That spirit needs to die.
Jesus did not come to sharpen our pride. He came to crush it at the cross.

Where Peninnah wounded, Christ heals.
Where Peninnah provoked, Christ invites.
Where Peninnah stood over the broken, Christ came near to them.

The good news is this: even if there is a Peninnah spirit hiding in us, Jesus does not only expose sin. He forgives it. He can tear cruelty out by the roots and give us a heart that weeps with those who weep. In Christ, the jealous can repent. The proud can bow. The sharp-tongued can become gentle. The one who wounded others can become a carrier of mercy.
So do not just read Peninnah as somebody else’s warning.
Read her as a call to repentance.
And read Hannah as a reminder that the God who sees tears is still writing redemptive endings.

Your pain is not invisible.
Your waiting is not wasted.
And the people who mocked you are not holding the pen.
Jesus is.

CTA:
Ask God to search your heart.

Key Scriptures:
1 Samuel 1:6–7
Romans 12:15
Luke 18:9–14
Ephesians 4:31–32
